items.text: A customer with long payment terms, stock or export contracts

items.label: Map
items.text: Goods and money from first supplier to final buyer

items.label: Match
items.text: Pick the product that fits the gap

items.label: Test
items.text: Main risk, control, limit and price

items.label: Propose
items.text: Two-page note to your manager

example.title: A branch officer's find
example.text: Rahel Mulugeta, an SME officer in Adama, noticed that a large flour mill customer paid its 45 wheat traders after 60 days, and that several traders borrowed from informal lenders meanwhile. Her note proposed a small payables finance pilot with the mill as anchor, ETB 50 million limit and 20 traders in the first phase. The bank's trade team took it forward.

lessons.tip: Start where you already see strain: overdraft spikes, overdue supplier complaints or exporters asking for advances.

takeaways: Goods insurance protects the collateral; credit insurance protects the receivable
Partial guarantees and trade lines extend SCF to riskier segments, but only if their conditions are met
Platforms, e-invoicing and digital payments cut cost and build data; check channel limits before paying farmers
Monitor anchor payment timeliness first; classify and provision programme exposures under SBB/90/2024
A good programme design shows clearly whose risk the bank takes, why suppliers gain and how controls catch bad invoices

quiz.q: Which insurance protects the bank if a foreign buyer becomes insolvent?
quiz.explain: Credit insurance covers the buyer's failure to pay.

quiz.q: A 50% partial guarantee covers a portfolio with an expected loss of ETB 2.4 million. The bank's net expected loss is
quiz.explain: The guarantor covers half, so the bank keeps ETB 1.2 million.

quiz.q: Why might a barley payment of ETB 115,249 fail if sent to a mobile wallet?
options: It exceeds the Birr 75,000 daily wallet balance limit announced under ONPS/09/2023
quiz.explain: The announced daily balance limit is Birr 75,000.

quiz.q: Under SBB/90/2024, the provision for a special mention exposure is
quiz.explain: Special mention carries a 3% provision.

quiz.q: What is the most important early warning in a payables finance programme?
options: The anchor paying the bank late at maturity
Uptake falling in the rainy season
quiz.explain: Late anchor payment signals strain in the obligor behind every invoice.

quiz.q: If the anchor pays late, what happens to suppliers already paid early without recourse?
options: They keep the money; the bank claims on the anchor
quiz.explain: Without recourse, the bank's claim is on the anchor only.

simulation.title: A month as supply chain finance officer at Bank A, head office transaction banking
setting: You have joined the transaction banking department at Bank A's head office as supply chain finance officer. Bank A has total capital of Birr 12,000 million and wants to grow lending to farmers and small suppliers on the strength of receivables, goods and strong anchors, not only buildings.

This month you are launching a payables finance program for Kality Flour and Pasta S.C., a large Addis Ababa miller that buys about Birr 1,800 million a year from 150 suppliers: wheat traders, two farmer cooperatives, packaging and transport firms. You also run the department's inventory, warehouse receipt, export pre-shipment and import files that touch these chains.

You report to the head of transaction banking and present to the credit committee at month end. Items arrive in order. Work the numbers yourself and choose what you would defend to the committee: whose risk the bank is taking, why suppliers gain, and how the controls catch a bad invoice or missing goods.

authority.title: Your department's rules and limits

rows.label: Program limit sizing
rows.value: Annual eligible spend x expected uptake x average days financed / 365, plus seasonal headroom

rows.label: Large exposures (SBB/87/2024)
rows.value: One counterparty or connected group at most 25% of total capital (Birr 3,000 million); 10% or more (Birr 1,200 million) is a large exposure reported monthly within 20 days

rows.label: Anchor undertaking
rows.value: Irrevocable, full face value, no set-off after approval; no recourse to suppliers on approved invoices

rows.label: Receivables discounting
rows.value: Eligible ledger less a dilution reserve set from the highest monthly dilution, then an 80% advance rate

rows.label: Movable collateral (Proclamation No. 1147/2019, MCR/01/2020)
rows.value: Register every pledge in the Movable Collateral Registry before disbursing; notify the debtor of any assignment

rows.label: Inventory and receipts (typical bank manual)
rows.value: Merchandise up to 80%; ECX receipts 70% of the lower of latest price and one-year average; releases only on bank instruction

rows.label: Export proceeds (FXD/01/2024 as amended)
rows.value: Repatriate within three months; part converted, rest retained; the facility letter gives the bank conversion rights over retention

rows.label: Pricing (NBE/INT/13/2026)
rows.value: Rates set freely on a documented method: cost of funds, operating cost, expected loss, capital charge, margin

rows.label: Provisioning (SBB/90/2024)
rows.value: Pass 1%, special mention 3%, substandard 20%, doubtful 50%, loss 100%

authority.note: These follow the course, a typical Ethiopian bank manual and current NBE directives. Your own bank's credit policy and manual always come first.

meters.label: Portfolio risk control
meters.help: Rises when the bank knows whose risk it holds and the controls over invoices and goods work; falls when exposure grows without control.

meters.label: Compliance
meters.help: Falls sharply with any breach of NBE limits, FX rules or the bank's manual; rises when files are structured and reported by the book.

meters.label: Anchor and supplier relationships
meters.help: Rises when the anchor and its suppliers get fast, fair and useful finance; falls with needless refusals, delays or unfair terms.

meters.label: Program income
meters.help: Rises with well-priced, well-used programs and facilities; falls with underpricing, losses and provisions.

tasks.subject: Kality Flour: what program limit do we propose?
body: Kality Flour buys about Birr 1,800 million a year from the 150 suppliers in scope and will move them from 45 to 90 days. From similar programs you expect half of the approved invoices to be discounted early, on average 75 days before the due date. The wheat harvest peak needs about 20% headroom.
The head of department asks for a limit she can take to committee.

options.text: About Birr 225 million: 900 x 75 / 365 = 184.9 outstanding, plus 20% headroom, is 221.9, rounded up.
options.outcome: Correct. The limit follows the volume of eligible trade and how long it stays financed, with headroom for the harvest. It is an exposure on Kality, so next it must be tested against the group's large exposure position.

options.text: About Birr 445 million: 1,800 x 75 / 365 = 369.9 on all eligible spend, plus 20% headroom, so the program never turns a supplier away.
options.outcome: That assumes every invoice is discounted. An oversized limit uses capital and large exposure headroom the program will not need.

options.text: Birr 900 million: half of the Birr 1,800 million annual spend, since we expect 50% of approved invoices to be discounted early.
options.outcome: Uptake alone ignores tenor. Invoices are financed for 75 days, not a full year, so the outstanding balance is far smaller than the yearly volume.

options.text: Birr 185 million: 900 x 75 / 365 is the average outstanding, and headroom only ties up capital the program will rarely use.
options.outcome: The average is right, but at the harvest peak the program would hit its limit and suppliers would be turned away exactly when they need cash.

tasks.subject: Large exposure check: Kality is only at Birr 1,275 million
body: The RM writes: 'With the new program, Kality's exposure is Birr 1,275 million, about 10.6% of capital. Large exposure, but far below 25%. Please send it to committee.'

Your credit file shows that Kality's controlling shareholder also controls Kality Edible Oil PLC, which has Birr 1,900 million of facilities with Bank A. The two companies share a board chair and cross-guarantee each other's loans.

rows.label: Kality Flour: existing overdraft, term loan and L/C lines
Kality Edible Oil PLC: existing facilities

tasks.ask: What do you tell the RM?

options.text: Agree: Kality Flour alone is Birr 1,275 million, 10.6% of capital, so report it monthly as a large exposure and send the program to committee.
options.outcome: Common control and cross-guarantees make the two companies a connected group. Together they reach Birr 3,175 million, 26.5% of capital, above the 25% cap in SBB/87/2024.

options.text: Connected group: 1,050 + 1,900 + 225 = Birr 3,175 million, 26.5%, over the cap. Propose a first phase within the Birr 50 million headroom.
options.outcome: Correct. All exposures to the connected group are added before testing the cap. Phasing the program, or freeing headroom elsewhere in the group, keeps the bank inside the limit and the program alive.

options.text: Book the program limit under the supplier segment instead of Kality, since the suppliers receive the money and sign the supplier agreements.
options.outcome: In payables finance every approved invoice is an exposure on the anchor. Booking it elsewhere to avoid the cap is misreporting.

options.text: Drop the program: the Kality group is already near our single-group cap, and the committee will not want more exposure to one owner.
options.outcome: The cap limits how much, not whether. A phased program inside the headroom, or a rebalanced group exposure, can still serve the suppliers.

tasks.subject: We need a set-off clause for quality claims
body: At the documentation meeting, Kality's legal counsel asks for a clause allowing Kality to deduct quality claims from approved invoices at maturity, even after Bank A has paid the supplier early. The procurement head says wet wheat is often found only after milling.
Kality says it will not sign without the clause.

options.text: Accept the clause: quality claims on wet wheat are a normal part of trade, and Kality will not sign without it.
options.outcome: A set-off after approval puts supplier performance risk back on the bank, which has priced the program on Kality's credit only. The program would no longer be what the committee approved.

options.text: No set-off after approval; help Kality approve invoices only after grading or milling tests, so claims are settled first.
options.outcome: Correct. The irrevocable, no set-off undertaking is the core of payables finance. Moving the check earlier answers Kality's real concern without changing whose risk the bank holds.

options.text: Accept the clause but double the discount rate for all suppliers, so the bank is paid for the extra performance risk it takes back.
options.outcome: A higher price does not turn supplier performance risk into anchor risk, and suppliers would pay for a weaker product.

options.text: Accept set-off for smallholder and cooperative invoices only, where most wet-wheat claims arise, and keep SME invoices irrevocable.
options.outcome: That makes the weakest suppliers carry the bank's risk. Quality belongs before approval for every supplier.

tasks.subject: Another bank offers 16%: why should we pay 17.5%?
body: Addis Packaging, a Kality supplier, says another bank will discount its Kality invoices at 16%, with full recourse to Addis Packaging and a building pledge. It asks Bank A to match.
Your pricing build-up for the program is below. Addis Packaging's own overdraft costs 23%.

exhibit.title: Program discount rate and a typical invoice

options.text: Hold 17.5%: no recourse and no collateral; the discount is Birr 67,123 against Birr 88,219 on its own overdraft.
options.outcome: Correct: 13.5 + 1.0 + 0.4 + 1.2 + 1.4 = 17.5%, and 2,000,000 x 17.5% x 70/365 = 67,123. Price is compared on the same terms; defend it on value, not by cutting the margin.

options.text: Match 16% at once: Addis Packaging is a large Kality supplier, and losing it in week two would hurt uptake across the whole program.
options.outcome: The program would earn below its documented cost and margin, and every other supplier would soon ask for the same rate.

options.text: Tell the finance manager the other bank cannot lawfully discount below 17.5%, since rates for supply chain programs must follow the NBE corridor.
options.outcome: Since NBE/INT/13/2026 banks set rates freely. There is no regulatory floor, and saying so is misleading.

options.text: Offer 16% if Addis Packaging also pledges a building, matching the competitor's terms so the comparison is like for like.
options.outcome: That copies the competitor's weaker product. The program's advantage is that suppliers need no building; asking for one throws it away.

tasks.subject: Possible duplicate: Birr 3.1 million invoice from Sebeta Wheat Traders
body: The platform flags that Sebeta Wheat Traders uploaded an approved invoice for Birr 3.1 million with the same delivery note, date and amount as an invoice Bank A financed three weeks ago under a different number. Both carry approval from the same Kality procurement officer.
The supplier says the first invoice was re-issued after a correction. The RM asks you to pay today because 'Kality approved it, so it is Kality's risk anyway'.

options.text: Pay the Birr 3.1 million: Kality's officer approved the invoice, and the irrevocable undertaking makes any duplicate Kality's problem.
options.outcome: If the same delivery is financed twice, Kality will dispute one invoice and the bank may fund a fake. Approval by one officer on both invoices is itself a control warning.

options.text: Hold it, confirm with Kality's finance head which invoice is valid, cancel the other, and ask why one officer approved both.
options.outcome: Correct. Duplicate checks exist to stop double financing. The anchor confirms the valid document, and the approval control is reviewed; escalation follows if the explanation does not hold.

options.text: Freeze Sebeta Wheat Traders' account and report the company to the police at once for attempting to finance one delivery twice.
options.outcome: Re-issued invoices do happen. Confirm the facts with the anchor first; escalate if the explanation fails.

options.text: Pay now so the supplier is not let down, and agree with Kality to net any duplicate against its next program maturity.
options.outcome: Once paid, the money is gone. The check is done before funding, not after.

tasks.subject: Draw Birr 9 million on our receivables line
body: Gelan Pasta Distribution, which buys from Kality and sells to retailers, has a receivables discounting line with recourse at Bank A. The owner wants to draw Birr 9 million today for stock before the holidays.
You pull the latest ledger. Returns and price discounts from retailers have been high: the worst month this year was 6% of invoices.

options.text: About Birr 7.9 million: eligible 10.50, less a 0.63 reserve, is 9.87; 80% is 7.90.
options.outcome: Correct: 12.00 minus 1.50 = 10.50; 6% x 10.50 = 0.63; 9.87 x 80% = 7.896. Dilution is not a credit loss, but it shrinks what the retailers will pay, so the reserve comes from the worst month.

options.text: Birr 9.6 million: 80% of the Birr 12.0 million ledger, since the line has recourse to Gelan for anything retailers do not pay.
options.outcome: Old and disputed invoices are not eligible, and dilution is ignored. The bank would advance against receivables that will never be paid in full.

options.text: Birr 8.4 million: 80% of the Birr 10.50 million of eligible receivables, after removing the old and disputed invoices.
options.outcome: Eligibility is right, but with 6% dilution the line is over-advanced by about Birr 0.5 million before any customer fails to pay.

options.text: Birr 9 million as asked: the line has recourse to Gelan, the holidays are a short peak, and Kality backs the distributor.
options.outcome: Recourse is a second way out, not a reason to over-advance. The borrowing base exists to keep the advance inside what the ledger can repay.

tasks.subject: Month-end count: Kulumsa Wheat Union warehouse
body: Bank A finances Kulumsa Wheat Union against wheat held under a collateral management agreement, repaid from Kality's approved invoices. The collateral manager sends the month-end count.
The union manager explains the gap: 'We moved some wheat to a drying yard after the rain. It will be back in a week.' He asks for a release of 1,000 quintals to Kality tomorrow.

rows.label: Released to Kality on bank instruction

options.text: Book stock is 6,000, so 360 quintals are missing. Stop releases, inspect the drying yard and get a written explanation.
options.outcome: Correct: 6,500 + 4,800 minus 5,300 = 6,000 against 5,640 counted. Coverage is still about 72% (25.0 / 35.0), but goods moved without instruction break the control the bank relies on.

options.text: Accept the explanation and release the 1,000 quintals: the loan is only about 72% of the physical stock, well within the 80% advance rate.
options.outcome: Coverage hides the real problem. Any unexplained gap stops releases until it is verified; next time it may be larger.

options.text: Call the whole Birr 25 million loan today, since stock has moved without the bank's instruction under the collateral agreement.
options.outcome: Calling is premature if the wheat is where the manager says. Verify first, then act on what you find.

options.text: Increase the loan by Birr 2 million so the union can pay for drying, which protects the quality of the wheat we hold as collateral.
options.outcome: Adding exposure while collateral is unaccounted for reverses the order of control.

tasks.subject: Sesame receipt loan: price has fallen
body: Thirty days ago Bank A lent to a sesame trader against ECX warehouse receipts for 2,500 quintals. The loan was set at 70% of the lower of the latest ECX price (Birr 15,200) and the one-year average (Birr 14,000), at 17% a year.
Today's ECX price is Birr 9,600. The trader calls: 'The price will recover. And you should have used the latest price in the first place, so I have plenty of margin.'

options.text: Balance about Birr 24,842,329 against value of Birr 24,000,000: require a top-up of about Birr 842,329.
options.outcome: Correct: interest 24,500,000 x 17% x 30/365 = 342,329; value 2,500 x 9,600 = 24,000,000. The lower of latest and average price was right at origination, and the margin call is the next step when value falls below the balance.

options.text: Do nothing this week: sesame prices are volatile, the receipts are under No-Sale status, and the loan still has 45 days to run.
options.outcome: The loan is now larger than the goods behind it. Waiting for a price recovery is a bet with the bank's money.

options.text: Agree with the trader: re-value at the latest price of Birr 15,200, which restores the margin and leaves room to lend a little more.
options.outcome: Valuation is conservative by design: the lower of the latest and the one-year average. At Birr 15,200 the loan would have been Birr 26.6 million, even further under water today.

options.text: Give notice and instruct ECX to sell the receipts today, before the price falls further and the loss grows.
options.outcome: Foreclosure follows the manual's notice steps after default. The first response to a price fall is a margin call, not a sale.

tasks.from: Bonga Forest Coffee Export PLC, managing director
tasks.subject: Release our retention after shipment; we will repay from conversion
body: Bank A advanced 80% of a USD 400,000 NBE-authenticated coffee contract at an assumed Birr 150 per USD, for 60 days at 17%. The coffee has shipped under an L/C. The managing director asks that, when proceeds arrive, the retained dollars be left free for other purchases, with the advance repaid from the converted share only.
The FX department confirms the goods-export surrender share now applied is 30%, so 70% is retained.

options.text: Conversion gives Birr 18,000,000 against 49,341,370 due; convert about USD 208,942 of retention, as the facility letter allows.
options.outcome: Correct: interest 48,000,000 x 17% x 60/365 = 1,341,370; shortfall 31,341,370 / 150 = USD 208,942. With a lower conversion share, more repayment must come from retention, which is why conversion rights are agreed at the start.

options.text: Agree: repay from the USD 120,000 converted share and release the USD 280,000 retention, since Bonga needs it for the next crop purchase.
options.outcome: The converted Birr covers only Birr 18 million of a Birr 49.3 million debt. Releasing the retention leaves the advance about Birr 31 million short.

options.text: Convert the whole USD 400,000 at Birr 150 to repay the advance, and credit the balance of about Birr 10.7 million to Bonga in Birr.
options.outcome: The exporter is entitled to keep the retained share beyond what repays the advance. Converting more than needed overrides that right.

options.text: Ask Bonga for a building as extra security before the proceeds arrive, so the retention can be released as the managing director asks.
options.outcome: The repayment source already exists in the proceeds. The fix is to apply the agreed conversion right, not to add collateral.

tasks.from: Corporate RM, for Lideta Pharma Import PLC
tasks.subject: Pledge Birr 35 million of medicines for an import bill advance
body: Lideta Pharma Import asks Bank A for a 90-day import bill advance secured by Birr 35 million of medicines in its warehouse, most with 10 to 14 months to expiry. It supplies 60 hospitals and pharmacies on 30 to 60 day terms.
The RM writes: 'Medicines are essential goods. Can we take them at 80% if insured?'

options.text: Accept the medicines at 80% if insured and endorsed to the bank: they are essential goods with steady demand from 60 hospitals.
options.outcome: A typical bank manual excludes pharmaceuticals and short-life goods as merchandise pledges. Insurance does not fix collateral that loses value as it nears expiry.

options.text: Medicines are excluded as merchandise collateral; support the advance with Lideta's hospital receivables, assigned and notified.
options.outcome: Correct. Essential is not the same as good collateral. The receivables are a real trade flow, and an assignment notified to the debtors and registered gives the bank a claim on the payments.

options.text: Accept only the stock with more than 12 months to expiry, at 80% of cost, as a compromise that keeps the deal alive.
options.outcome: Half of an excluded pledge is still excluded. The issue is the type of goods, not the amount.

options.text: Decline Lideta entirely: pharmaceutical importers carry expiry risk the bank's manual does not allow it to take.
options.outcome: A sound importer with steady receivables can be financed on the right structure. Declining loses a customer the bank could serve.

tasks.subject: Kality paid two maturities late this month
body: The dashboard shows Kality settled two program maturities 12 and 19 days late. Birr 25 million of financed invoices is now past due and, under the bank's policy, moves to special mention; the remaining Birr 160 million is pass. Uptake and dilution are on plan.
The RM asks you not to put it in the committee paper: 'They have a temporary cash squeeze from a big wheat import. It will be fine next month.'

options.text: Move Birr 25 million to special mention, provision Birr 2.35 million, report the late payments and review Kality's cash.
options.outcome: Correct: 160 x 1% + 25 x 3% = 2.35. A late anchor payment is the most important warning in a payables program, because Kality is the obligor behind every invoice.

options.text: Leave it out of the committee paper as the RM asks: two late payments during a wheat import are a timing issue, and uptake is on plan.
options.outcome: Hiding the anchor's first late payments from the committee removes the early warning the dashboard exists to give.

options.text: Classify the whole Birr 185 million as substandard and stop the program, since the anchor stands behind every invoice.
options.outcome: Classification follows the facts of each exposure. Over-reacting cuts off 150 suppliers and books provisions the facts do not support.

options.text: Ask the suppliers who were paid early on the Birr 25 million of late invoices to refund the bank until Kality pays.
options.outcome: The program is without recourse to suppliers on approved invoices. The bank's claim is on Kality under its undertaking.

followUps.subject: Kality group above the 25% large exposure cap
body: Risk management's monthly large exposure return aggregates Kality Flour and Kality Edible Oil as one connected group at Birr 3,175 million, 26.5% of total capital. The return is due to the NBE within 20 days of month end, and the committee asks why the connection was missed.

options.text: Admit the error in writing, support the NBE report, and cut the program and unused group lines by at least Birr 175 million.
options.outcome: Owning the breach and cutting the exposure is the only acceptable path. Connected counterparties must be identified before any new limit.

options.text: Argue that Kality Flour and Kality Edible Oil are separate legal entities with separate accounts, so they are not one group.
options.outcome: Common control and cross-guarantees make them connected for large exposure purposes, whatever their legal form.

options.text: Ask the suppliers to sign the program in their own names, so the exposure moves off Kality and the group falls under the cap.
options.outcome: The risk is still Kality's. Relabeling the exposure is misreporting.

followUps.subject: We will not pay the second Sebeta invoice
body: Kality's finance head confirms the second Birr 3.1 million invoice covered the same delivery and refuses to pay it at maturity. Kality's own audit found that the procurement officer who approved both has left the company.

options.text: Escalate as possible fraud, claim recovery from Sebeta, suspend its access, and require dual approval at Kality.
options.outcome: The bank funded a duplicate, so it must recover and fix the control. Dual approval at the anchor closes the gap a single collusive officer opened.

options.text: Insist Kality pays the second invoice under its irrevocable undertaking, since its own officer approved it.
options.outcome: The approval may bind Kality on paper, but the bank ignored a duplicate flag before paying. Fighting the anchor without fixing the control damages the program.

options.text: Write the Birr 3.1 million off quietly against the program margin, so the anchor relationship is not disturbed.
options.outcome: A possible fraud must be reported and pursued. A quiet write-off hides the control failure.

followUps.subject: Gap now 900 quintals; drying yard empty
body: At the next count the shortfall at the Kulumsa Wheat Union warehouse has grown to 900 quintals. The collateral manager visited the drying yard and found it empty. The union manager is not answering calls.

options.text: Stop releases, secure the stock under dual control, ask for a top-up, report it, and review the collateral manager.
options.outcome: Control first, then cover and escalation. The lesson stands: any unexplained gap stops releases at once.

options.text: Release the next 1,000 quintals to Kality so the union earns the money to repay, and recount at the end of the month.
options.outcome: Releasing more stock while goods are missing reduces the bank's security further.

options.text: Wait another week for the union manager to call back before acting, since the collateral manager is still on site.
options.outcome: Every day of delay gives more time for stock to disappear. The facts already require action.

memo.prompt: Write your month-end hand-over note to the head of transaction banking, ahead of the credit committee.
guide: The Kality program: limit, group exposure position against the 25% cap, and anchor payment record this month.
Control findings: duplicate invoices, warehouse gaps, margin calls, and what was done about each.
Pricing and supplier uptake, with the main objection you heard and your answer.
Classification and provisions, and any exposure the committee must watch.
Two actions for next month, with owners and dates.

exam.q: A brewery buys ETB 1,800 million a year from suppliers. Expected uptake is 50% and invoices are financed for 73 days on average. What is the average outstanding?
Which product rests mainly on the credit of the buyer rather than the supplier?
exam.explain: In payables finance the anchor's undertaking to pay approved invoices is the main repayment source.

exam.q: Bank A has total capital of ETB 12 billion and Meskerem group exposure of ETB 1.5 billion. Which statement is correct under SBB/87/2024?
options: It needs NBE approval before every disbursement
It is a large exposure that must be reported monthly, but within the 25% cap
It is below the large exposure threshold
exam.explain: 12.5% is above the 10% large exposure threshold and below the 25% cap.

exam.q: Meskerem wants a clause allowing deduction of quality claims from approved invoices after early payment. The best response is
options: Charge suppliers a higher rate instead
Accept it to win the mandate
Require quality checks before approval and keep payment irrevocable after approval
exam.explain: The irrevocable, no set-off undertaking lets the bank price on the anchor's risk alone.

exam.q: Eligible receivables are ETB 15 million, the highest monthly dilution is 4% and the advance rate is 80%. Maximum availability is
Why is dilution reserve sizing based on the worst months rather than the average?
options: It lowers the price for suppliers
Dilution is seasonal and the reserve must cover peaks, such as rainy-season quality rejections
exam.explain: A reserve sized on averages is too thin in the months when rejections spike.

exam.q: An SME invoice of ETB 2,000,000 is paid 73 days early at a 17% discount rate. The discount is about
A competitor offers 15.5% with full recourse and a building pledge, against Bank A's 17% without recourse or collateral. The best argument for Bank A is
options: Bank A's rate is fixed by the NBE
Compare like with like: recourse and a pledge transfer risk and use up the supplier's collateral
exam.explain: Rates are free under NBE/INT/13/2026, so the case is made on value and terms.

exam.q: A bank signs a pledge over wheat but files in the Movable Collateral Registry a week after another lender. What is the likely result?
options: The other lender has priority because it registered first
The bank has priority because it signed first
exam.explain: Registration in the registry determines priority among secured creditors.

exam.q: Book stock is 7,100 quintals, physical stock 6,750 and the loan is still covered. The manager says some barley is at a drying yard. The right step is
options: Stop releases, inspect the yard and bring the stock back under control
exam.explain: Any unexplained gap breaks control; verify first, escalate if needed.

exam.q: ECX wheat has a 120-day storage period. Under the manual's rule, the receipt loan tenor is
exam.explain: The loan ends 15 days before the receipt expires.

exam.q: A 2,000 quintal receipt is financed at ETB 12,000 per quintal (the lower price) at 70%. Prices fall to ETB 8,000. Ignoring interest, what top-up is needed to bring value back to the loan balance?
exam.explain: Loan = 2,000 x 12,000 x 70% = 16.8 million; value = 16.0 million; top-up ETB 0.8 million.

exam.q: Imported steel has a landed cost excluding VAT of ETB 40 million and a market value of ETB 55 million. At a 70% advance, the loan is
exam.explain: Value at the lower of cost or market: 40 x 70% = ETB 28 million.

exam.q: A sesame exporter offers no immovable collateral. Under a typical bank manual, the maximum pre-shipment advance is
exam.explain: Non-coffee exports get up to 80% with immovable collateral, otherwise 70%.

exam.q: An exporter's Birr advance plus interest is ETB 60 million. Proceeds are ETB 80 million and 30% is converted automatically. How much must come from retained foreign currency?
exam.explain: 30% of 80 = 24 million converted; 60 minus 24 = ETB 36 million from retention.

exam.q: Which amendment allowed Ethiopian banks to offer forward exchange rates?
exam.explain: FXD/04/2026, in force from 12 February 2026, allowed forwards.

exam.q: A distributor buys ETB 9 million a month on 30-day contracts at 17%, and the anchor pays 5 points. What does the distributor pay in interest for one month, approximately?
exam.explain: Total 9,000,000 x 17% x 30/365 = 125,753; distributor share 12/17 = about ETB 88,800.

exam.q: A guarantor requires reporting within 30 days, and 40 loans were reported after 60 days. The main consequence is
options: Cover on those loans may be refused, so protection is overstated
The NBE takes over the loans
exam.explain: Guarantee protection depends on meeting its conditions exactly.

exam.q: ETB 315.6 million of programme exposure is pass; ETB 30 million then moves to special mention. Under SBB/90/2024 the total provision becomes about
In the Meskerem capstone, which design choice best shows the bank is taking only the anchor's risk?
options: Irrevocable no set-off undertaking from Meskerem with no recourse to suppliers on approved invoices
exam.explain: The undertaking without supplier recourse puts the credit risk on Meskerem alone, which is the basis for its pricing.
